intro: Look at the edges around the glasses and mug. Some tools make broad fields of color, while others reveal a picture one narrow line at a time.
alt: Four portraits in thick oil pastel, soft airbrush color, white scratchboard lines and blue-gray markers.

variants.name: oil pastel
variants.look: Thick violet and coral strokes catch on the paper, leaving bright crumbs of color.
variants.history: Pigment held in wax and nondrying oil forms a pastel that can be blended and layered.
variants.when: Make a close portrait where you want an emphatic record of pressure and gesture.
variants.why: Its oily binder helps strong colors layer and smear into one another.

variants.name: airbrush art
variants.look: Smooth cyan and magenta gradients soften nearly every edge.
variants.history: Compressed-air paint sprayers became common tools in commercial illustration and retouching during the 20th century.
variants.when: Render a glowing surface or a soft shadow around a hard object.
variants.why: Fine droplets can build an even gradient without brush marks.

variants.name: scratchboard
variants.look: Thin pale scratches stand out against a black ground.
variants.history: Commercial illustrators used prepared boards with a light layer under black ink, scratching the top layer away for white marks.
variants.when: Make a black-and-white image with strongly lit threads, hair or fabric.
variants.why: Carving highlights out of the ground leaves a powerful silhouette and a crisp white line.

source.label: Georgia Museum of Art | Scratchboard art

variants.name: marker rendering
variants.look: Broad parallel chisel-tip marks overlap in the jacket and background.
variants.history: Felt-tip pens became widely available in the 20th century and color markers found a place in design studios and architectural rendering.
variants.when: Sketch a product, room or costume quickly with a small set of colors.
variants.why: Transparent strokes make it easy to build up a darker value without waiting for paint to dry.

prompt: Create one square atlas comparison plate, precisely four independently composed equally sized artwork squares in full-bleed 2x2 grid, hard splits on both midlines, no margin nor gutter. Show the framed character holding her coffee at an easel, identical waist-up composition. Use the attached illustration only as subject character reference. 30-year-old attractive ash-blonde woman with tidy low bun, black rectangular eyeglasses clearly visible in every panel, tailored charcoal knee-length business dress under fitted blazer, signature white coffee mug with small four-color windowpane mark and plain blue lanyard with a blank badge. Never reproduce the card border or typography. The artwork techniques differ dramatically. Put nothing that crosses the splits. No letters, words, numerals or panel labels anywhere. TOP LEFT: crumbly thick oil pastel in violet/coral/ochre on grainy paper, short visible strokes and painterly clumps. TOP RIGHT: airbrushed illustration with glowing turquoise-magenta seamless transitions and soft shadows. BOTTOM LEFT: scratchboard with only white scraped parallel lines revealing form in an almost completely black field, bold cut highlights. BOTTOM RIGHT: architect's marker rendering on white with translucent parallel warm gray and blue overlapping chisel-tip strokes.
